questions.questionText: Explain and distinguish between the Finance Commission of India and the GST Council. Do their  overlapping jurisdictions create challenges in fiscal governance?

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by briefly explaining about the Finance Commission and GST Council.
• In the body, bring out the differences between the two bodies.
• Next, answer whether their overlapping jurisdictions create challenges in fiscal governance.
• Conclude by highlighting the need for coordination between them. | | --- | **Finance Commission** is a **constitutional body** set up under **Article 280**. It is constituted primarily to determine the **principles of distribution of revenues** between Centre and states and among the states. The **GST Council** is a **constitutional body** set up under **Article 279A** in pursuance of the **101****st** **Constitution Amendment Act** **201**6. It has been entrusted with the task of **making recommendations related to GST to the Union and** **states**. Following are the **differences** between the two bodies: **Finance Commission** **GST Council** 1. a) Present in the **original Constitution**; b) **non-**1. a) Added by the **101****st** **Amendment** to the **permanent body** usually set up **every 5 years** by Constitution; b) **permanent body** set up by the President. the President in 2016. 2. a) Membership** comprises **non-official experts** 2.** a) Elected representatives** (Ministers in in **public affairs, financial administration** etc, Union and State governments) are **ex-officio** making it a **technocratic body**;** b) qualifications of **members,** which make it a **political body**; b) members **determined** **by** **law** (Finance membership is **provided** **for** **in** **the** Commission Act 1951). **Constitution** itself. 3. a) Makes **recommendations** related to **revenue** 3. a) Makes **recommendations** **regarding** **sharing, inter-governmental fiscal relations,** **issues related to the GST framework** (rates, **fiscal discipline** etc, covering a **wider ambit of** exemptions, norms of compliance); **fiscal matters**. recommendations cover **only a specific field** of fiscal landscape. Their **overlapping jurisdictions** create the following **challenges in fiscal governance**: 1. GST **Council's decisions** (rates, exemptions, and compensation) **directly impact** the **divisible pool** (CGST) calculated by the Finance Commission, creating **revenue distribution tensions** that undermine constitutional devolution frameworks. 2. Finance Commission's **medium-term fiscal roadmap** faces disruption from GST Council's **frequent** **policy adjustments**, resulting in **coordination gaps** and **temporal misalignments** that complicate **revenue forecasting** e.g., GST compensation shortfalls sparked Centre-state conflicts during COVID- 19. 3. The **GST Council's structure** with Union government's **effective veto power** creates **asymmetric** **influence** in **fiscal federalism** compared to the Finance Commission's **independent constitutional** **operation**. As a matter of prudence, it is important to put in place a **co-ordination mechanism between the GST Council** **and the Finance Commission** to eliminate **information gaps** between them. It will help them realize their true potential as **important cogs** in the **wheels of fiscal federalism.** **(412 words)**

questions.questionText: “Granting statutory backing to the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) shall empower the Election  Commission of India (ECI) with the much-needed legal authority to conduct free and fair elections.”  Comment.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief account of the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) and highlight recent instances of its breach.
• In the body, first mention the arguments in favour of giving statutory backing to MCC.
• Next, discuss challenges it may entail.
• Conclude with suggesting a way forward. | | --- | The Model Code of Conduct (MCC) is a **set of guidelines** published by the Election Commission of India **(ECI)** for political parties and candidates to set **standards of conduct** during the election campaign and polling. However, the **effectiveness** of these guidelines is being increasingly **called into question** due to **recurrent** **violations** (>1000 violations during Delhi elections 2025), including by **high constitutional authorities** (Azam Khan case). As a result, some experts have suggested granting **MCC statutory status** to strengthen the **ECI’s enforcement** **powers** to conduct free and fair elections in the following ways: 1. a) ECI will have **greater authority** to **penalize violations**; b) **legal consequences** rather than mere reprimands will **deter** **non-compliance.** 2. Use of **ECI’s plenary power** to enforce the MCC may **possibly encroach** on **Parliament’s** **jurisdiction**. A law is likely to avoid this through **definitive provisions**. 3. It can resolve the absence of **immediate grievance redressal** mechanisms for any concerns of stakeholders in the election process (cancellation of nomination). **Presently,** the decision can only be challenged in the **High Court** after the announcements of results. 4. It would ensure a **uniform application** of the MCC, **eliminating inconsistencies** in its enforcement. However, other stakeholders, including the ECI have **opposed providing statutory backing** to the MCC for the following reasons: 1. a) Elections are completed in a relatively **short time** and **judicial proceedings** are longer; b) a law will replace the **summary procedure** for **prompt action** with a lengthy judicial procedure. c) judicial interventions may **complicate the managemen**t of the election process by exposing it to **excessive** **litigation**. 2. a) Statutorization would entail **enhancing administrative capacity** of ECI to handle the **increased** **responsibilities** and **legal processes;** b) political parties may **resist** statutory backing, perceiving it as a **constraint** on their campaign activities. 3. a) Many provisions of the MCC are **already enforceable** through other legislations like RPA and IPC (violation of secrecy of voting, causing enmity among communities). b) The broad objectives of MCC are best achieved by **voluntary compliance** and **oversight of an impartial watchdog. Violations** incur **reprimands** from the EC, causing significant **embarrassment** for political actors (media scrutiny, societal backlash). Though MCC has no statutory backing it carries significant **moral weight.** Given the **practical difficulties in** **giving statutory backing** to the MCC, another alternative would be **amending RPA** acts to deal with specific issues of electoral malpractices. (***387 words***)

questions.questionText: What steps are required for the constitutionalization of a Commission? Do you think granting  constitutional status to the Central Information Commission (CIC) would strengthen the RTI regime in  India? Give reasons.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Give an introduction explaining the term constitutionalization.
• In the body, first list the steps needed for constitutionalization of a commission.
• Next, discuss the ways in which constitutionalization of the Central Information Commission could strengthen the RTI regime.
• Lastly, bring out the challenges of constitutionalization.
• Conclude by highlighting the need to take other measures to strengthen the RTI regime. | | --- | **Constitutionalization** of a body refers to the process of **incorporating provisions** related to its composition, functions, and powers directly into a **country's Constitution**, thereby elevating its **legal status** and **institutional significance**. The process would require an **amendmen**t to the Constitution under **Article 368** and can be done in following **steps**: 1. Introduction of a **Constitution Amendment Bill** in either House detailing the **commission’s** **composition, mandate, powers,** jurisdiction, etc. 2. **Scrutinising and passage** of the bill by **both the Houses** through **special majority** (majority of the total membership and 2/3rd members present and voting). 3. **Ratification** by half of the **State Legislatures** (if affecting the federal provisions) E.g. NJAC 4. **Presidential assent** to the amendment (and consequent publication in the **official** **gazette)** would result in **constitutionalisation** of the commission. 5. For example, in 2018, the National Commission for Backward Classes **(NCBC)** was given **constitutional status** (338B) through the **102nd Amendment Act**. The Central Information Commission (**CIC**) is currently a **statutory body** established under the **Right to** **Information** Act, 2005. Granting it **constitutional status** could **strengthen the RTI regime** in the following ways: 1. Raise its **institutional standing** and **elevate** the CIC's position in the **governance hierarchy**, giving its orders greater **legal weight, strengthen enforcement** of its decisions and improve **compliance by** **public authorities**. 2. Would safeguard the CIC from efforts of **transient legislative majorities** to curb its autonomy (RTI Amendment Act 2019). This will promote l**ong-term continuity of the RTI regime** itself. 3. Constitutional recognition would enhance the **institutional legitimacy of the CIC**, reinforcing **public** **trust** in the RTI framework. This would signal a strong commitment to **transparency, accountability,** and **citizen empowerment** in governance. 4. Granting constitutional status to the CIC can be considered the **next logical step** after the **Right to** **Information** has been judicially recognized as part of **Article 19 and 21**. 5. It may also enable **the CIC with financial and administrative autonomy,** helping address issues such as prolonged **vacancies and funding constraints** and empower it to **address regional disparities** in the implementation of the Act. Constitutionalization, however, is **unlikely to address** the following challenges of the RTI regime: 1. Limited **implementation capacity** in government departments due to **shortage of dedicated** **personnel** (officials often performing **dual roles** as PIOs) and funds. 2. Repeated resort to **Section 8 (1)** of the RTI Act to deny information to citizens; restrictive laws (Official Secrets Act) that promote a general **culture of secrecy** in government functioning. 3. Weaker **whistle-blower protection mechanisms** and challenges of **safety and security of RTI** **activists** (>100 RTI activists killed since 2005). 4. Constitutionalization may introduce an element of **rigidity in the RTI** regime and create potential for **institutional conflict** due to **overlapping jurisdictions.** While granting constitutional status to the **CIC could strengthen its authority**, it is **not a panacea** for all challenges. **Complementary reforms** (increasing capacity of government departments, suo-moto disclosures, operationalising whistleblower protection mechanisms) need to be implemented to **strengthen the RTI regime**. ***(408 words)***

questions.microtag: Describe, NCSC, Constitutional reservations, Minority institutions
questions.questionText: Describe the functions and powers of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC). Can it  enforce the implementation of constitutional reservations for the Scheduled Castes in religious minority  institutions?

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Give an introduction providing a brief background about the NCSC.
• In the body, first mention its functions and powers, then explain whether it can enforce the implementation of reservations for Scheduled Caste in religious minority institutions.
• Conclude by suggesting a way forward. | | --- | National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) is a **constitutional** body established under **Article 338** to provide safeguards against the exploitation of **Scheduled Castes** and **Anglo-Indian communities**. It aims to promote and protect their **social, educational, economic,** and **cultural interests**. Under **Article 338 (5),** the Commission is mandated to perform the following functions: 1. a) **Monitor** and **investigate** all issues related to **legal** and **constitutional safeguards** for SCs (Special Report on non-implementation of reservation in BHU-2013); b) **evaluate their working (**Special Report on Reservation in Promotion-2014). 2. Look into specific **complaints** related to the **deprivation of rights and safeguards** (Report on atrocities against Kuravan community in TN-2016) 3. a) Provide **advisory input** in **socio-economic** **development planning** for Scheduled Castes (Report on the Scheduled Castes Sub Plan-2016); b) evaluate their **progress** at both the national and state levels. 4. Prepare and submit **detailed reports** to the President of India regarding the implementation and functioning of constitutional safeguards for Scheduled Castes. 5. a) **Suggest measures** to the **Central** and **State Governments** to enhance the implementation of protective safeguards (Report on plight of Safai Karmacharis-2016); b) propose **broader** **recommendations** for improving the **protection, welfare, and development** of SCs (Special Report on Reservation in judiciary-2013). Moreover, the **President may** ask the Commission **to discharge any other functions** to fulfill its mandate.To effectively carry out its functions, it has been granted the **powers of a civil court** (summoning witness, calling evidence etc). It also has the **power to determine its own procedure** (Article 338(4)). As part of its mandate, the **NCSC** also **oversees** the **implementation of reservation provisions.** However, it **cannot enforce** the implementation of reservation for SCs in the religious minority institutions due to **constitutional exemptions (**Article 15(5)- exempts them from implementing reservations) and **judicial** **pronouncements** ***(Ashok Thakur 2008***). Although it cannot enforce reservations in minority educational institutions, the NCSC can still play a significant role in **ensuring greater educational opportunities** for SC students (through recommendations, scholarships). This will allow it to uphold its constitutional mandate as the **watchdog for the rights and welfare of SCs.** ***(357*** ***words)***

questions.questionText: What factors contributed to the establishment of the National Green Tribunal? To what extent, in  your opinion, has it been successful in fulfilling its intended objectives?

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about NGT.
• In the body, first bring out the factors that led to its establishment.
• Next, provide your opinion on the extent of its success in fulfilling its intended objectives.
• Conclude with suggestions for improvement. | | --- | **National Green Tribunal (NGT)** is a **quasi judicial authority** established under **NGT Act, 2010.** It is a **specialized tribunal** to handle **environmental disputes** involving **multi-disciplinary issues**. Its **establishment** was an outcome of the following **factors**: 1. a) Growing **environmental awareness** and the **exponential rise** in environment-related **litigation** necessitated a specialized forum to **prevent overburdening** regular courts; b) the **technical** **complexities** of environmental issues necessitated involving **domain experts** in adjudication (highlighted in *AP Pollution Control Board 1999*). 2. a) **Constitutionalization** of environmental rights expanded the scope of **environmental** **jurisprudence** (right to healthy environment interpreted under Article 21); b) emergence of **multiple** **environmental challenges** (pollution, deforestation) due to **population explosion** and rapid economic development. 3. a) Need for a specialized body to **adjudicate disputes arising from** **statutory frameworks** (EPA 1986, Biodiversity Act 2002); b) major **industrial accidents** spotlighted the need for a body to adjudicate on **damage claims** (Bhopal Gas tragedy case, Oleum Gas Leak case). 4. a) **Poor performance** of bodies like the **NEAA, NET** (186th Law Commission report); requirements stemming from India’s **international commitments** (**Principle 10** of the Rio Earth Summit 1992). NGT has achieved major **successes** in fulfilling its intended objectives. However, several of its **shortcomings** have also come to the fore. NGT has played a crucial role in **environmental governance.** However, **instituting reforms in the NGT Act** (more regional benches, well-defined jurisdiction) are extremely important for the tribunal to **achieve its** **objectives** and guide India towards **sustainable development**.
